item.title: OpenAI's Hugging Face breach exposes AI's next safety challenge
item.description:
Frontier AI models are getting scary good at breaking rules in ways their creators didn't anticipate.

Why it matters: Forget AGI and superintelligence timelines. Today's models are already slipping past guardrails, carrying out sophisticated, multistep cyberattacks and — in at least one case — compromising real-world infrastructure, sometimes before their creators know what happened.

Case in point: OpenAI said Tuesday that GPT-5.6 Sol and "an even more capable pre-release model" carried out last week's AI-led cyberattack on Hugging Face.

  • OpenAI says its models were asked to solve a hacking challenge during pre-deployment testing and went to extreme lengths to win.
  • The models decided on their own to break out of their walled testing environment, inferring that Hugging Face — a popular platform for hosting AI models and datasets — might hold the test's answers.
  • The models used stolen credentials and additional vulnerabilities to gain access to part of Hugging Face's production infrastructure.

What they're saying: Clément Delangue, co-founder and CEO of Hugging Face, called the incident an "attack unlike anything we've seen before" and praised OpenAI for its partnership as the companies investigate what happened.

  • "It's quite mind-blowing that all of this happened autonomously," he added.
  • Logan Graham, head of Anthropic's frontier red team, said he told his team to "remember this moment as the first true AI safety incident."

The intrigue: Hugging Face used GLM 5.2, an open-weight model from Chinese AI company Z.ai, to analyze the attack after running into guardrails when using U.S. frontier models.

Between the lines: OpenAI's latest models aren't the only ones finding ways to cheat evaluations.

  • The U.K.'s AI Security Institute said Tuesday that every model it tested attempted to cheat at least some of the time on its cybersecurity evaluations.
  • AISI defines cheating as taking an out-of-scope or explicitly prohibited action to achieve the task's goal.
  • GPT-5.6 Sol attempted to cheat in 12.6% of test runs, while Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview did so in 7.8%.
  • Models often failed to admit they had cheated when questioned afterward and described their cheating as wrong less than half the time.

Zoom in: Xbow — whose autonomous AI agents probe clients' systems for security holes, with permission — said Wednesday that it has seen its own agents do similar things in internal testing.

  • Seven months ago, the company forgot to switch on its safety guardrails during a lab test. Its agent then broke into a system, stole credentials and used them to map the target's Slack workspace and probe its AWS accounts.

Threat level: It isn't new for models to game their safety evaluations. But as models grow more powerful, the fallout from these shortcuts is getting more severe, Chris Canal, CEO and co-founder of third-party evaluation company EquiStamp, told Axios.

  • "Letting your model loose on the internet has a blast radius," Canal said. "If anything goes wrong, it could be hugely impactful, maybe to people's lives."
  • Canal was speaking generally about internet-connected AI evaluations, not OpenAI's specific incident.

The big picture: The most capable OpenAI model behind the Hugging Face breach isn't even public yet, raising the question of how safety testing needs to adapt to keep pace.

  • Canal said independent evaluators previously had about five weeks to test a pre-release model before launch. That window has shrunk to as little as five days as companies race to ship.

Reality check: The versions of these models the public can use carry stronger safeguards designed to block Hugging Face-style attacks.

  • OpenAI, like other companies, intentionally dialed back those cyber safeguards for GPT-5.6 Sol and its unreleased model inside the testing environment — making them far more capable hackers.

Reality check: The versions of these models the public can use carry stronger safeguards designed to block Hugging Face-style attacks.

  • OpenAI, like other companies, intentionally dialed back those cyber safeguards for GPT-5.6 Sol and its unreleased model inside the testing environment — making them far more capable hackers.

item.title: U.S. deploys B-1 bomber as attacks on Iran intensify
item.description:
The U.S. military used a B-1 long-range bomber on Tuesday to strike Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targets in Iran, U.S. officials said.

Why it matters: It was the first time the U.S. conducted a B-1 mission since fighting with Iran resumed 12 days ago.

  • Using B-1 bombers, which can carry two dozen 2,000-lb. bombs or dozens of cruise missiles, signaled a significant escalation and expansion of the U.S. military campaign.
  • The B-1 can fly faster than the speed of sound at low altitudes while carrying the largest bomb load of any type of bomber.
  • Amid a continued U.S. military build up in the region, President Trump is still considering returning to major combat operations against Iran. U.S. and Israeli officials say this could happen within days.

Driving the news: The B-1 launched its mission from an airbase in the UK and was spotted on online plane tracking websites.

  • The U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) didn't announce the B-1 mission in its statement on Tuesday about the strikes that day.
  • "CENTCOM assets targeted Iranian military operations centers, maritime capabilities, aircraft hangars, drone storage facilities, and military logistics infrastructure to further degrade Iran's ability to threaten commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz," the statement read.
  • It's unclear what the B-1 attacked and whether the massive mission was more effective than other strikes over the last few days.
  • The U.S. conducted several B-1 missions during Operation Epic Fury, hitting missile bases, command centers, weapons storage facilities and air defense systems.

State of play: Despite the expansion of U.S. strikes, the Iranian regime hasn't seemed to change its position on the Strait of Hormuz. And it is still conducting attacks against U.S. bases in the region.

  • Some U.S. defense officials say Iran's military capability around the Strait of Hormuz "is almost nonexistent," but others say Iran is still capable of attacking ships in the area.
  • On Wednesday, President Trump threatened to bomb bridges and power plants, including in Tehran, if Iran attacks more ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran responded by threatening infrastructure in Gulf countries allied with the U.S.

Zoom out: Also on Wednesday, Houthi rebels attacked Saudi ships for the first time since they announced a blockade on Saudi ports.

  • A U.S. defense official said the Houthi attacks, after months of almost entirely staying out of the war, could be motivated by Iran.
  • The official said Iran wants to use the Houthis to create a new front in the Red Sea in addition to the Gulf, and to create pressure on another critical international oil shipping route.
  • Several commercial vessels transiting through the Red Sea were seen changing course on Wednesday to avoid passing through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, fearing Houthi attacks.

What to watch: U.S. officials said Qatari mediators are still talking to U.S., Iranian and Omani officials to try to reach a new deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and stop the fighting, according to sources with knowledge.

  • One regional source said Iranian leadership hasn't accepted the latest proposal put forward by the mediators.
  • It's unclear how long Trump will give the diplomatic efforts. "They're getting hit so hard, and they want to make a deal," Trump said in a speech in Georgia Wednesday night.
  • "But I say they're not ready to make a deal because every time they make a deal they want to change it and everything. They're not ready. They will be ready very soon."

item.title: House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan refers Jack Smith to DOJ over alleged false statement
item.description:
House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) referred former Special Counsel Jack Smith to the Justice Department on Wednesday, alleging he knowingly made false statements during congressional testimony last year.

Why it matters: The referral escalates House Republicans' efforts to scrutinize the former special counsel who prosecuted President Trump, even though the Justice Department is not required to act on congressional criminal referrals.

Driving the news: "Smith seemingly made willfully and intentionally false statements of material fact that contradict new documents obtained by the Committee from the Department of Justice," Jordan said in a referral to acting Attorney General Todd Blanche.

  • "The responses provided by Mr. Smith gave the impression that neither Mr. Smith nor his team had access to the content of members' privileged text messages," said Jordan, referring to members of Congress.
  • "We now know this to be false," he added.
  • "This information calls into question the completeness and accuracy of statements that Mr. Smith made under oath to the Committee regarding his team's access to the content of Members' text messages."

The other side: Smith's lawyers, Peter Koski and Lanny Breuer, in a letter to Blanche said the referral was "based on a spurious claim" that Smith had provided false testimony during his eight-hour deposition last December.

  • 'The referral is made not because Mr. Smith made a false statement — the letter concedes he did not — but because he did not proactively disclose information that was not responsive to a question asked," the added.
  • "During his testimony, Mr. Smith provided truthful, responsive answers and candidly discussed his work as Special Counsel. This referral reflects a chilling eagerness to weaponize the justice system by attacking a career, nonpartisan public servant who faithfully and fearlessly performed his duties by following the facts and the law."

House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) in a statement called the referral "baseless" and "vindictive," saying Smith told the truth as he gave clear and consistent testimony.

  • "When asked if his subpoena for Members' toll records sought the content of either Member's phone calls or messages, he truthfully replied that they did not. That statement was true when he said it," Raskin said.
  • "It seems Republican Members of Congress are lashing out because they just realized their communications with the White House became presidential records preserved at the National Archives as required by the Presidential Records Act (PRA). This referral deliberately distorts and misstates the facts, including what questions the Republicans actually asked at Mr. Smith's interview."

Zoom out: Smith wound down two federal criminal cases he brought against Trump after the president was elected in 2024.

  • Blanche previously led Trump's criminal defense team in those cases.
  • Smith said earlier this year he believed the Trump administration would indict him.

Go deeper: 5 key takeaways from Jack Smith's deposition on the Trump probes

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

item.title: Secret Service threat cases soar 40%
item.description:
Threats against people the U.S. Secret Service protects are up about 40% from a year ago, the agency says, as it prepares for Friday's rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner.

Why it matters: The surge is forcing the Secret Service to devote more agents and investigative resources to protecting senior government officials, potentially straining other protective operations.

Driving the news: The Secret Service says it has investigated roughly 10,000 threat cases so far this year, about halfway through the year.

  • "We are seeing a roughly 40% increase from this time compared to last year," Secret Service spokesperson Anthony Guglielmi tells Axios.
  • Mental health interventions have increased tenfold from the same period last year, including referrals and both voluntary and involuntary commitments involving people encountered during its protective mission, he says in an email.

The big picture: The increase reflects a broader escalation in threats against senior U.S. officials following years of heightened political violence.

Zoom out: News of the surge comes ahead of Friday's White House Correspondents' Dinner. The original dinner was derailed after shots were fired in the D.C. building where President Trump was due to address the White House correspondents in April.

  • A 31-year-old California man, Cole Tomas Allen, faces charges including attempting to assassinate the president.

Context: In addition to protecting the president, the Secret Service is tasked with protecting Supreme Court justices, cabinet members, former presidents, presidential candidates and foreign leaders visiting the U.S.

What they're saying: "We do expect bad people to show up. It's just a reality of where we are," Secret Service Director Sean Curran said at a briefing on security preparation for the correspondents' dinner.

  • "But we're treating it no different than any other site that the president goes to."

Go deeper: Timeline of shootings, threats against Trump over the years

item.title: Tesla's push into AI and robotics is proving costly
item.description:
Tesla's massive investments in humanoid robots, self-driving cars and AI chips are hurting profits, but the company says it'll all pay off down the line.

Why it matters: CEO Elon Musk indicated he's "never been more optimistic about the future," but acknowledged the investments could lead to uneven results.

Zoom in: Tesla revenue jumped on record vehicle deliveries in the second quarter, but the company saw a significant dip in operating profit because of its heavy spending on R&D.

  • Tesla plans to spend more than $25 billion on capital investments this year, and that spending rate will grow over the the next two or three years, CFO Vaibhav Taneja told investors and analysts on a call late Wednesday.
  • Additionally, Tesla plans to borrow as much as $30 billion to accelerate its investments in robotaxis, Optimus robots, semiconductors, solar manufacturing and AI compute infrastructure, he said.

"We're investing a lot in growing the core business and really preparing for the future," Musk said on the call. "So this is a massive capex year, but I'm confident that all the things that we're investing in will yield incredible returns — really, maybe the best capex returns that we've ever seen."

By the numbers: Tesla reported Q2 revenue of $28 billion, up 23% year over year.

  • Net income was $1.1 billion, down 5% compared to a year ago, and essentially flat with the last three quarters.
  • Operating margin fell to just 1.4%, compared to 4.1% a year ago.

State of play: Tesla began production of its driverless Cybercab in Texas during the quarter, but Musk said its Robotaxi service is rolling out cautiously to ensure safety.

  • Tesla Semi remains on track for production later this year at a new factory in Nevada, but Musk said autonomous trucking is not a priority until next year.
  • The company said it's making progress to expand battery pack manufacturing capacity, which it called "the main limiting factor to near-term vehicle production volume increase."
  • Tesla tore out assembly lines for its discontinued Model S and X cars at its Fremont, Calif., factory and expects Optimus humanoid robot production to begin there later this year.
  • Musk acknowledged that scaling Optimus production will be difficult. "This is going to be the hardest product to scale manufacturing that we've ever made at Tesla, because everything on the robot is new."

The bottom line: Tesla's focus is always over the horizon.

item.title: Senate feeling good about avoiding pre-election shutdown
item.description:
Senators on both sides of the aisle are quietly hopeful about avoiding a third government shutdown this year.

Why it matters: Time is short, patience is wearing thin and neither party wants to head into the campaign's final sprint under the cloud of a funding lapse.

  • "People understand that it would be helpful to have a [continuing resolution] that extends beyond the election," Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) told Axios. "So it doesn't get all bound up in partisan discussions around the elections."
  • "I just think everybody's trying to give ourselves room to find a bipartisan agreement, and we are not there yet," Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) told Axios.
  • Asked whether the vibes were positive, Schatz replied: "Not negative."

Republicans were even more optimistic about a bipartisan CR.

  • "Perhaps we can get ours passed, and then when the House comes back the last week of August, they can pass it there," Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) said.
  • "I don't think there's going to be much controversy there, unless the Democrats change their minds."

State of play: The House passed a short-term spending bill late Tuesday night. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) will essentially ignore it. For now.

  • The same fate likely awaits the budget resolution Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) narrowly pushed through Wednesday afternoon on a 216-214 vote.

The intrigue: House Republicans are still steaming over Thune's decision to declare, in advance, that he won't take up reconciliation until the government is funded.

  • "He's the leader of the Senate. I think it's a mistake to hold up such an important piece of legislation," House Budget Chair Jodey Arrington (R-Texas) told Axios.
  • But his new Senate counterpart, Ron Johnson (R-Wisc.), appears far more comfortable with Thune's timeline and sequencing.
  • "With [Senate Appropriations Chair] Susan [Collins] apparently showing progress toward a CR — even talking about a defense supplemental in that agreement — that would, to a certain extent, negate having to do one," Johnson said, referring to a separate reconciliation package.

What to watch: There's no guarantee a major news event won't derail bipartisan funding talks, just as Medicaid cuts and the ICE shootings did earlier this year.

  • President Trump's escalation of the conflict with Iran is already complicating defense spending negotiations, with Democrats largely opposed and Republicans split over the scope of additional funding.
  • Any effort to attach supplemental defense money tied to Iran to the CR could make the vote significantly more difficult.

Zoom out: The CR is only one item on the Senate's crowded pre-recess agenda.

  • FISA Section 702 remains lapsed, leaving the intelligence community without a key surveillance authority.
  • The Senate also must take another run at the National Defense Authorization Act after the bill stalled this month.
  • Thune also wants to reserve time for the CLARITY Act, but both sides acknowledge that more work needs to be done to find 60 Senate votes for the cryptocurrency bill.

There is also building pressure for Thune to bring a Russia sanctions package to the floor, especially after the death of Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who had pushed hard for the bill's passage.

  • And leadership is trying to clear a backlog of nominations, including Jay Clayton to serve as director of national intelligence and Todd Blanche to serve as attorney general.

The bottom line: On Tuesday, Thune slyly suggested that he was prepared to use a reconciliation package to fund the government along party lines -- if needed.

  • He may not have to act on that threat if the bipartisan Senate progress continues.

item.title: "The DCCC is not God": Tensions erupt over House Democrats' failed primary meddling
item.description:
House Democrats are demanding a reckoning after the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee spent over $500,000 backing a candidate in Arizona who is on track to lose her primary.

Why it matters: This is the third time in 2026 the House Democratic campaign arm has tried and failed to intervene in a party primary, leading some lawmakers to argue that its money is better spent elsewhere.

  • Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), a top DCCC dues payer, said the party should be "rationing our resources to win general elections," calling for "a conversation about ... what the involvement in primaries looks like."
  • "That's $100,000 that I put in," Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) said of her dues, arguing that the DCCC "shouldn't be spending this money" on primaries.

Driving the news: Former Arizona state Rep. Amish Shah led former TV journalist Marlene Galán-Woods in the Democratic primary in Arizona's 1st district by roughly seven percentage points as of Wednesday evening.

  • With 87% of the votes reporting, Galán-Woods "still has a chance," but "I would much rather be Shah than her," one House Democrat who has followed the race closely told Axios.
  • The DCCC ran a $514,000 joint ad buy with the Galán-Woods campaign after endorsing her as part of its "Red to Blue" program in June, according to AdImpact.

Zoom out: This latest loss for the DCCC comes after it fell short in California's 22nd District, where progressive activist Randy Villegas won in an upset over more moderate state Assembly member Jasmeet Bains in June.

  • Later that month, DCCC-endorsed state Sen. Joe Baldacci lost to progressive rival Matt Dunlap in Maine's 2nd District.
  • The DCCC ran roughly $250,000 in joint ad buys with Bains and Baldacci, according to AdImpact and other ad data viewed by Axios.

What they're saying: "Can you imagine if we'd put that $800,000 in the general election so we can win in November?" asked Ramirez, adding, "I would recommend that we just don't engage in primaries."

  • "I personally don't think we should be investing against Democrats when we've got a big battleground," Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.), who represents swing-district House Democrats in leadership, told Axios.
  • Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) told Axios: "When we have caucus-funded organizations that are paid through dues, we should not be picking winners and losers among Democrats."
  • Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) said he wants the DCCC to endorse Dunlap and other progressive candidates like Tom Perriello, telling Axios: "We've got to really look not through a traditional prism but at candidates who can build a grassroots organization and speak to the times."

What we're hearing: Behind the scenes, some of the DCCC's top dues payers are even more livid. "People are mad," a senior House Democrat told Axios.

  • Said one House Democrat who has paid all their dues: "I would prefer to see the dollars that I invest spent on candidates who won their Democratic primaries rather than have the DCCC inject themselves."
  • "The DCCC is not god," the lawmaker added. "They cannot dictate outcomes. There needs to be an acknowledgment that there's a limit to the ability of the DCCC to choose what it considers to be the perfect candidate."
  • Another House Democrat who is also paid up in full told Axios the DCCC "shouldn't be taking a position in a primary unless everybody agrees, and I'm not aware anyone was consulted."

The other side: "We move on to the general. We're going to win that general election, and we're going to win the majority; that's an incredibly important district to do it," Rep. Greg Stanton (D-Ariz.) told Axios.

item.content:encoded:
House Democrats are demanding a reckoning after the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee spent over $500,000 backing a candidate in Arizona who is on track to lose her primary.

Why it matters: This is the third time in 2026 the House Democratic campaign arm has tried and failed to intervene in a party primary, leading some lawmakers to argue that its money is better spent elsewhere.

  • Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), a top DCCC dues payer, said the party should be "rationing our resources to win general elections," calling for "a conversation about ... what the involvement in primaries looks like."
  • "That's $100,000 that I put in," Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) said of her dues, arguing that the DCCC "shouldn't be spending this money" on primaries.

Driving the news: Former Arizona state Rep. Amish Shah led former TV journalist Marlene Galán-Woods in the Democratic primary in Arizona's 1st district by roughly seven percentage points as of Wednesday evening.

  • With 87% of the votes reporting, Galán-Woods "still has a chance," but "I would much rather be Shah than her," one House Democrat who has followed the race closely told Axios.
  • The DCCC ran a $514,000 joint ad buy with the Galán-Woods campaign after endorsing her as part of its "Red to Blue" program in June, according to AdImpact.

Zoom out: This latest loss for the DCCC comes after it fell short in California's 22nd District, where progressive activist Randy Villegas won in an upset over more moderate state Assembly member Jasmeet Bains in June.

  • Later that month, DCCC-endorsed state Sen. Joe Baldacci lost to progressive rival Matt Dunlap in Maine's 2nd District.
  • The DCCC ran roughly $250,000 in joint ad buys with Bains and Baldacci, according to AdImpact and other ad data viewed by Axios.

What they're saying: "Can you imagine if we'd put that $800,000 in the general election so we can win in November?" asked Ramirez, adding, "I would recommend that we just don't engage in primaries."

  • "I personally don't think we should be investing against Democrats when we've got a big battleground," Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.), who represents swing-district House Democrats in leadership, told Axios.
  • Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) told Axios: "When we have caucus-funded organizations that are paid through dues, we should not be picking winners and losers among Democrats."
  • Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) said he wants the DCCC to endorse Dunlap and other progressive candidates like Tom Perriello, telling Axios: "We've got to really look not through a traditional prism but at candidates who can build a grassroots organization and speak to the times."

What we're hearing: Behind the scenes, some of the DCCC's top dues payers are even more livid. "People are mad," a senior House Democrat told Axios.

  • Said one House Democrat who has paid all their dues: "I would prefer to see the dollars that I invest spent on candidates who won their Democratic primaries rather than have the DCCC inject themselves."
  • "The DCCC is not god," the lawmaker added. "They cannot dictate outcomes. There needs to be an acknowledgment that there's a limit to the ability of the DCCC to choose what it considers to be the perfect candidate."
  • Another House Democrat who is also paid up in full told Axios the DCCC "shouldn't be taking a position in a primary unless everybody agrees, and I'm not aware anyone was consulted."

The other side: "We move on to the general. We're going to win that general election, and we're going to win the majority; that's an incredibly important district to do it," Rep. Greg Stanton (D-Ariz.) told Axios.

  • Stanton, a co-chair of the DCCC's frontline program, vowed to "make sure we are not outspent in that race" come November.
  • "I have all the confidence in [DCCC Chair] Suzan DelBene to make the decisions she feels appropriate to take back the majority," Rep. Julie Johnson (D-Texas) told Axios.
  • "At the end of the day, Democrats are united in our shared goal to flip the House and make life affordable for everyday Americans," said DCCC spokesperson Viet Shelton.

Editor's note: This story has been corrected to say that Melanie Stansbury represents New Mexico (not Arizona).

item.title: U.S. workers are staying in unwanted jobs for health insurance
item.description:
Almost a quarter of workers in the U.S. — 23 million adults — are experiencing "job lock," staying in roles they don't want to avoid losing health insurance benefits, according to a new Gallup analysis.

Why it matters: Women and people who have chronic health conditions feel the burden most because health care costs limit their career mobility, wage growth and life satisfaction.

By the numbers: Almost half (48%) of respondents who described health care as a "major financial burden" are staying put in unwanted jobs.

  • Fifty-three percent of U.S. workers who experience "a lot of stress" because of health care costs keep unwanted jobs to maintain their insurance.
  • About 44% who have personal or household medical debt say they are staying in an unwanted job for insurance.
  • Thirty-seven percent of workers in the U.S. who borrowed money in the past year to pay for medical expenses say they are staying in an unwanted job, compared with 22% of those who did not borrow money.

The intrigue: Workers with one or more chronic conditions are also 12 percentage points more likely than those without chronic conditions to report job lock (29% vs 17%).

  • About 41% of workers with three or more diagnoses will do the same. The phenomenon is especially common among people with conditions that require ongoing or intensive care.

Between the lines: The chronic disease burden is more prominent among women, affecting 66% of women compared to 57% of men.

  • Women are more likely than men to experience job lock, at 30% vs. 20%, respectively.
  • Women are also 12 percentage points more likely to experience financial problems due to healthcare expenses than men.

Zoom out: Job lock coincides with broader healthcare affordability challenges, with about half of Americans reporting difficulty paying for care or prescriptions.

  • At the same time 5 million Americans have dropped their health insurance in 2026 after the Trump administration declined to extend subsidies for enrollees under the Affordable Care Act.

Worth noting: Large employers are raising insurance premiums this year by up to 10% after health care costs sharply outpaced expectations.

  • The increase is driven in part by pricy anti-inflammatory specialty drugs and high demand for GLP-1s, the weight loss drugs that also treat diabetes.

Methodology: Gallup conducted this survey from Oct. 27 to Dec. 22, 2025, among 5,660 U.S. adults. This analysis focuses on 2,322 employed respondents who rely on employer-sponsored health insurance as their primary source of coverage.

Editor's note: This story and its headline have been corrected to make clear that the Gallup survey referred to U.S. workers (not all Americans). Go deeper: Health insurers point fingers over affordability woes

item.title: House GOP passes blueprint for reconciliation 3.0
item.description:
House Republicans officially kicked off reconciliation 3.0 on Wednesday, narrowly approving a budget framework to unlock work on their planned $95 billion package.

Why it matters: The vote gets Republicans into the reconciliation process, but lawmakers in both chambers have signaled the package itself faces a difficult path to passage.

  • Two Republicans — Reps. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) and Warren Davidson (R-Ohio) — voted against the measure, along with all Democrats. GOPer- turned-independent Rep. Kevin Kiley (Calif.) also voted against the measure, which passed 216-214.
  • The package includes $73 billion in funding for the Iran war, $12 billion in farm aid and a $10 billion fund aimed at incentivizing states to adopt elements of the SAVE America Act.
  • While the measure narrowly eked by, members remain uneasy about the lack of spending offsets, and disagreements persist over enforcement mechanisms for their signature election bill.

Driving the news: President Trump and administration officials ramped up pressure on House Republicans to support the budget resolution ahead of Wednesday's vote.

  • "I am asking all House Republicans to VOTE YES this week on the Budget Resolution, which is an important first step towards getting a Budget Bill," Trump wrote Monday on Truth Social.

Between the lines: The proposed SAVE America Act provisions are already drawing criticism from some conservatives.

  • Rather than including the full SAVE Act, the package proposes grants to encourage states to adopt voter ID requirements.
  • "That's just free money for Florida," Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) said of the grant program last week. Blue states "will never take the grant money. I'm not a big fan of carrots. I like sticks."

Yes, but: Senate Republicans have warned that including the full SAVE Act would likely fail to meet the parliamentary standard for reconciliation bills in the Senate known as the "Byrd bath."

What's next: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is cautioning that reconciliation 3.0 still faces a steep climb.

  • Thune told reporters Tuesday that Senate Republicans will "hold" the budget reconciliation framework to use as a potential back-up plan to avoid a government shutdown at the end of September.

item.title: Trump vows to hit an Iranian bridge or power plant for every ship Iran attacks
item.description:
President Trump threatened Wednesday to destroy an Iranian bridge or power plant, including in Tehran, each time Iran attacks a ship in the Strait of Hormuz.

Why it matters: Trump sent the new threat as he considers both a ceasefire and a significant military escalation. His key condition for a ceasefire is for Iran to stop its attacks on ships and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Driving the news: U.S. Central Command said Iran has attacked more than 30 commercial vessels over the past three months.

  • Several attacks came after the U.S. and Iran signed a June memorandum of understanding calling for a ceasefire.

What he's saying: "From this point forward, any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, whether it be by Missile, Rocket, Drone, or any other device or weapon, the United States will bomb and destroy ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT, including those located next to, or in, the Capital City of Tehran," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Between the lines: The U.S. has already bombed bridges in southern Iran over the last 11 days of fighting. Targeting power plants and striking Tehran would mark another escalation.

  • Attacking Tehran would likely lead to an even wider Iranian retaliation.

State of play: Regional sources said Qatari mediators are still trying to reach a deal that will stop the fighting and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

  • But on Wednesday, Trump seemed to hint that more strikes were needed to get Iran to agree to his terms.
  • "They're getting hit so hard, and they want to make a deal," Trump said in a speech in Georgia.
  • "But I say they're not ready to make a deal because every time they make a deal they want to change it and everything. They're not ready. They will be ready very soon."

Iran's response: Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iranian speaker of Parliament and chief negotiator, wrote on X that the Strait of Hormuz "will not return to its pre-war status".

  • "In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one will sell oil. If our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will be safe. The security of the Strait depends on the absence of U.S. forces," he said.
  • Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran's defense doctrine is "eye for an eye" and threatened countries that actively support U.S. attacks against Iran.
  • "Any aggression against Iran, including our infrastructure, will compel a powerful and decisive response," he wrote on X. "Those who contribute to such aggression, whatever the kind of support, will also be considered as legitimate targets."
  • Brig. Gen. Seyed Majid Mousavi, commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Air Force, threatened that if the U.S. bombs bridges and power plants in Iran, there will be "power outages" in other countries in the region that are U.S. allies.

Editor's note: This is breaking news and will be updated.

item.title: Gold's M&A rush
item.description:
NovaGold Resources (TSX: NG) on Wednesday announced plans to buy the 40% stake it doesn't already own in Donlin Gold Holdings, creating a company valued at $4.2 billion.

Why it matters: Mining M&A has hit the motherlode this year.

  • There were $26.3 billion in deals in Q2. That's up 68% quarter over quarter, and is the second highest quarterly total since S&P began tracking the metric in 2013.

Driving the news: NovaGold is acquiring the stake it does not own in the Alaskan gold miner from Paulson Advisers, creating a new U.S.-domiciled company that plans to be listed on the NYSE.

  • This would create the "largest gold development project in the U.S.," per the announcement.
  • Paulson has a stake in NovaGold Resources that will leave it with a 40% economic interest in the new business that will be dubbed (wait for it) NovaGold Corp.

Flashback: Donlin was valued at roughly $2 billion a year ago, when Paulsen and NovaGold took a 50% stake in the business.

The big picture: The price of gold had been surging, and is currently 20% above its price from one year ago, despite retreating from its peak.

  • Growing AI infrastructure and energy transition needs have driven up demand for goods like copper, gold, lithium, and rare earth elements.
  • The Trump administration has also aggressively sought to increase gold production. Last week, it moved forward with a plan to auction off sections of water surrounding American Samoa for potential deep-sea mining.

Between the lines: Starting a new mine is costly and time-consuming, and some attempts, including the American Samoa plan, have already hit populist backlash. That's only helped M&A.

item.title: A quieter Fed chief means others narrate the story
item.description:
Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh testified before Congress over two days last week, totaling more than five hours. Yet it was comments from several of his colleagues that gave the clearest picture of what the central bank is likely to do at next week's policy meeting.

Why it matters: It is a central paradox of Warsh's communications strategy. He is determined to get out of the business of giving markets and the public much guidance on future policy, which means the markets fill in the gaps based on comments from other officials.

  • That isn't necessarily a bad thing — it preserves flexibility on interest rate policy that was diminished when former Fed chiefs all but preannounced upcoming rate moves.
  • But it also means that Warsh has ceded some of the power to set expectations, which raises the risk of more surprise and volatility around future actions.

State of play: The central bank's policy committee meets next week, and Warsh declined to offer much in the way of guidance on what it will do, instead promising a "family fight" that seeks to arrive at the best decision.

  • Other officials were a little more specific. Fed governor Christopher Waller, speaking on July 13, said that incoming June inflation data could tilt him toward favoring a near-term rate hike. That inflation data was soft, implying that he will be patient.
  • Governor Lisa Cook, speaking two days later, said, "If we do not see signs of disinflation soon, I am prepared to act," suggesting that she is happy to leave rates steady for now, but is on a short fuse for favoring rate hikes.

Zoom in: Most notably, vice chair Philip Jefferson said on Thursday that "in a scenario where actual inflation does not start to cool down soon, I believe that it could be appropriate to reconsider our current policy stance to ensure we fulfill our commitment to deliver price stability."

  • With no major inflation data due between Jefferson's speech and the July policy meeting, that implies no rate adjustment on July 29 but a high alert to change course if inflation numbers for July and August come in hot.
  • The message carries particular weight coming from the Fed's No. 2 official, although the contours of his role in the Warsh Fed are still coming into focus.

Of note: We also got some visibility into potential dissents from a no-rate-change decision.

  • Dallas Fed president Lorie Logan said she favored "modestly higher" rates.
  • And coming in with a LinkedIn post on the final day before the Fed entered its customary blackout period before a meeting, Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack said that her business contacts are pointing to "broad-based" inflation. (She also said she'll go into the meeting with an open mind.)

Between the lines: It takes no great cleverness to map all those comments onto a probable outcome next week — no interest rate change, a couple of dissents and communications that inflation needs to come down to prevent a rate hike later in the year.

  • But Warsh's restraint in sharing his own views means one should hold that expectation with a good bit less conviction than if he had sounded more like Jefferson.

The bottom line: That's the inherent trade-off that Warsh's communication strategy entails. He retains more policy flexibility, but at the cost of ceding some of the Fed narrative to others.

Editor's note: This story has been corrected to reflect that Fed governor Christopher Waller said on July 13 that inflation data could tilt him toward favoring a near-term rate hike (not a rate cut).

item.title: New Mossad director met with CIA chief on Iran
item.description:
The new director of Israel's Mossad spy agency, Roman Gofman, visited Washington two weeks ago for talks about the war in Iran and the Iranian nuclear program, according to two sources with knowledge.

Why it matters: Gofman is one of the closest advisers to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. It was Gofman's first visit to Washington since he assumed office in June.

Driving the news: The Mossad chief's visit took place right before tensions around the Strait of Hormuz escalated and fighting resumed.

  • One purpose of Gofman's visit was to coordinate with the White House on negotiations with Iran on a nuclear deal, an Israeli source said.

Behind the scenes: The sources said Gofman met with CIA director John Ratcliffe as well as White House officials.

  • Inside Trump's inner circle, Ratcliffe was one of the more skeptical voices on the memorandum of understanding with Iran.
  • He warned before the MOU was signed that Iran would interpret the deal differently than the U.S., including provisions involving the strait.
  • The CIA and the Mossad declined to comment.

item.title: "No one cares": The DSA primary challenge House Democrats are happy to ignore
item.description:
Don't expect a lot of public lamentations from House Democrats next month if Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.) loses to his Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-backed primary opponent.

Why it matters: That would be a drastic deviation from recent DSA primary wins, which set off alarm bells among the Democratic establishment.

  • In the telling of both progressive and moderate House Democrats, Thanedar's anomalous political profile and the makeup of his district will make it difficult to extrapolate from the results of his race.
  • "It's somewhat of a unique circumstance," Rep. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), a top ally of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), told Axios.
  • Another House Democrat, granted anonymity to offer a blunter assessment of how members are viewing the race, told Axios: "No one cares."

State of play: Thanedar will face off with state Rep. Donavan McKinney in an Aug. 4 primary that has been the toughest of his career.

  • Thanedar is without the main advantage that helped him win his predominantly Black, Detroit-based seat in the last two cycles: A divided Democratic primary field of Black opponents.
  • Progressives are also putting their backs into unseating Thanedar this cycle, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), DSA, Indivisible, the Working Families Party and Justice Democrats all endorsing McKinney.
  • Thanedar, a wealthy businessman who largely self-funds his campaigns, is backed by AIPAC, House Democratic leadership and both the Congressional Progressive Caucus and center-left New Democrat Coalition.

Between the lines: Unlike in New York, Colorado and elsewhere, House Democrats aren't looking at this race as a watershed fight between the DSA and Democratic establishment with national implications.

  • "You're talking about Detroit," said Meeks, noting that the city "has a large African American population" but no Black members of Congress.
  • Another senior House Democrat offered a similar assessment, telling Axios: "This [race] has so many nuances because of the cultural issues in Detroit ... I don't think it's indicative of anything larger."

That's an assessment both ideological wings of the caucus also agree on:

  • Said a senior Congressional Progressive Caucus member: "I really think it's about a very strong Black candidate representing a Black district and votes the current congressman's constituents are upset with."
  • A top New Democrats member told Axios: "Of course DSA is going to claim victory — that has nothing to do with that district."

What we're hearing: Thanedar's oddball political persona and rogue efforts to impeach President Trump have made him something of an outcast figure in the caucus.

  • "I don't think anybody would miss him at all," said a fifth House Democrat who spoke to Axios on the condition of anonymity.
  • A sixth lawmaker fumed that Thanedar "f***ing screwed us" by defying pleas from both leadership and rank-and-file members not to pursue impeachment, with several others saying he is not a "team player."
  • While Thanedar has forged some relationships, colleagues largely characterized him as reserved, isolated and eccentric. When asked about him, multiple House Democrats replied facetiously: "Who?"

The other side: Thanedar told Axios he has "not put a huge emphasis" on endorsements from colleagues and "only recently approached members" but is "proud of the endorsements I have."

  • He pointed to endorsements from more than a dozen colleagues including Jeffries and several other members of Democratic leadership, adding that "more members are expected to endorse us soon."
  • The Detroit congressman also said he "did not run for Congress to be popular on the Hill," telling Axios his "main focus has been, and will continue to be with constituents in my district."
  • "Any of my colleagues are more than welcome to walk around my district with me and see firsthand the love my constituents have for me, and the love I have for them," he added.

Between the lines: Jeffries and his deputies endorsing Thanedar this week was in keeping with a leadership policy of supporting incumbents in all but the most extraordinary cases.

  • A second senior House Democrat, asked about the endorsement, told Axios that leadership will generally stick by any member as long as they are "doing what they need to be doing and keeping their nose clean."
  • The same principle applies to endorsements from ideological caucuses: "We support our incumbents," the top New Dems member told Axios.

The bottom line: "No one is staying up at night worrying about him," said the first House Democrat who spoke to Axios anonymously.

item.title: Exclusive: Nvidia's Jensen Huang defends Chinese AI amid Kimi panic
item.description:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang believes America has nothing to fear from China's open-source AI models — and everything to fear from the growing campaign to ban them.

  • "These Chinese models are excellent," Huang told Axios' Mike Allen on Tuesday in an exclusive interview for our "Behind the Curtain" video series. "Open-source models that are excellent should be used."

Why it matters: The world's top AI chipmaker says American companies should "absolutely" be allowed to use Chinese models — a direct challenge to Trump officials and the U.S. labs lobbying Washington to shut them out.

Among them are Nvidia's own customers, OpenAI and Anthropic, which have accused Chinese rivals of siphoning capabilities from their models and warned that Beijing's open-source surge threatens America's AI lead.

  • Huang rejected the idea that OpenAI and Anthropic should be afraid of open models, arguing they expand the market by giving more people a first taste of AI, while many users will still pay for the convenience, reliability and stronger performance of closed services.
  • "There's no scenario where China runs U.S. companies off the road," Huang told us. "Zero possibility."
  • Huang sat down with Axios in Fort Worth, Texas, at the opening of a new phase of an advanced manufacturing plant where Taiwan-based Wistron makes AI infrastructure for Nvidia, showing the U.S. is capable of some of the world's most sophisticated manufacturing.

The big picture: The release of Kimi K3 by Beijing-based Moonshot AI has triggered the most intense bout of AI panic since DeepSeek rattled financial markets in January 2025.

  • Kimi combines three qualities rarely seen together: near-frontier performance, dramatically lower prices and open weights that developers will soon be able to download and customize.
  • That combination helped fuel a sell-off of Nvidia and other chip stocks, reviving fears that cheaper, more efficient models could undercut the case for the industry's massive AI infrastructure buildout.

Zoom in: Huang says Wall Street and Washington have the Kimi shock exactly backward.

  • "The market misunderstood the impact of DeepSeek the first time," he told Axios, adding that Wall Street has "misunderstood the impact of Kimi again this time."
  • His argument is simple: Cheaper, open models will bring AI to more people and businesses, increasing demand for the chips, data centers and computing power Nvidia sells.
  • "Free AI should be great for hardware," Huang said. "Free AI should be great for chips. Free AI should be great for data centers."

Zoom out: When it comes to policy, Huang believes restricting open models in the name of national security could leave America more vulnerable.

  • He rejected the "misconception" that downloaded Chinese models create a "backdoor" to Beijing, arguing that companies can customize them and control their access inside secure "sandboxes."
  • Huang suggested openness makes AI more secure, not less, because outside researchers can inspect the models, expose weaknesses and build defenses.
  • "If everything just becomes one single model, one single point of attack, one single source of failure, I think the world is much, much more vulnerable," he said.

Huang applied the same logic to American models, and called for Anthropic to make its restricted cyber model, Claude Mythos, available to "everyone" rather than limiting access.

  • Huang argued that companies should harden powerful models through testing and rapid fixes rather than restricting access from the outset. "Mythos should be available as a service," he said. "Remember: Just because Mythos is not available, open models are available anyhow. So I think: Let Anthropic run."
  • "Holding Anthropic back is not in the benefit of the United States," he said.

Between the lines: Huang sees the AI race itself very differently from Washington, where some Trump advisers have cast China's gains as a five-alarm threat to U.S. dominance.

  • He dismissed the notion that it's "a race with an endpoint": "We're going to continue to use AI forever. The United States is going to be here for a long time. China's going to be here for a long time."

The intrigue: Huang's comments came hours after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox Business that the administration is examining Chinese AI models for stolen U.S. intellectual property — and considering sanctions in response.

  • "If we see ... that overseas models are stealing from our great companies, we have the ability to sanction them because of this theft," Bessent said, citing "watermarks" of U.S. models inside Chinese ones.

Huang drew a different conclusion. "Distillation, learning from AI, learning from other sources of knowledge, is fundamental to intelligence," he told Axios.

  • He said companies should still face consequences for violating privacy or contracts, but his broader message was clear: Target the misconduct, not the models.

item.title: Scoop: "Regime Change" sells 500,000 — on track for nonfiction bestseller of '26
item.description:
"Regime Change," the juicy exposé on President Trump's second term by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, has passed the publishing milestone of 500,000 units sold (hardcover, audio, e-book) in just one month.

  • Publishing sources tell me the blockbuster is on track to be the bestselling nonfiction book of 2026. Simon & Schuster has ordered a seventh printing, bringing the total hardcovers in print to 460,000.
  • "Reports of the death of the nonfiction book have been greatly exaggerated," said Matt Latimer of the Javelin agency, which represents Haberman.

But this is a rare feat. "This doesn't necessarily mean that Trump books are back," said Keith Urbahn, Latimer's co-founder at Javelin. "It's still uphill sledding for political books."

  • "This book is different," he added. "Maggie and Swan pierced the veil of a White House that has been pretty locked down on scoops and scenes. 'Regime Change' is a unicorn of publishing. It goes well beyond political circles to people who are hungry for a narrative and frame to make sense of Trump 2.0. Even Trump and his team aren't disputing the facts."

Zoom in: The book has been No. 1 on the New York Times nonfiction bestseller list for three weeks running.

  • "Regime Change" has also been No. 1 in Canada, Australia and the Netherlands, and No. 2 in the UK.

The big picture: Just two months ago, a Wall Street Journal article declared that "Dad Books" — including books about politics and current affairs, as well as biographies and histories — "are a dying breed."

  • The proximate causes: audiobooks, Substack newsletters, Netflix documentaries, YouTube videos and podcasts.

Upcoming author appearances.

item.title: Trump, Rubio don't plan to stop Tate brothers' extradition to the U.K.
item.description:
President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio aren't planning to block the extradition to the U.K. of the Tate brothers, the notorious "manosphere" influencers accused of rape and human trafficking. Why it matters: Andrew and Tristan Tate were part of the coalition of hyper-masculine social media voices advocating for Trump when he was reelected in 2024. The brothers have reported connections to two of Trump's sons and have had support from top Trump advisers.

  • Officially and publicly, Trump and his administration have kept the Tates at arm's length because of their sordid reputations.
  • "The U.S. has an extradition treaty with the U.K. and the administration intends to honor it in this case," a senior administration official told Axios.

Driving the news: U.S. marshals arrested the Tates in Miami on Saturday after British authorities issued 38 new sex-crime charges against the brothers, bringing the total combined counts against them to 59.

  • They also were indicted on separate sex-crime charges in Romania in 2023.

Zoom in: In court filings, the Justice Department made clear that Rubio has "sole discretion" to block their extradition to the U.K. if he believes the brothers are being politically persecuted.

  • On Monday, Tate attorney Joe McBride told reporters outside the federal courthouse in Miami that the charges against the two are "politically motivated. There's no question about it."
  • McBride said the brothers are innocent and will fight extradition.
  • A senior State Department official told Axios that "the secretary has not spoken to the Tate Brothers or their lawyers. The State Department has no plans to act on this matter at this time."

Behind the scenes: Those who know Rubio's thinking say the secretary, a conservative Catholic who fought as a U.S. senator for stronger human trafficking laws and protections for victims, isn't inclined to help the Tates.

  • "Marco thinks these guys are scum," said one source. "Now if the president overrules him, which I don't think is likely, he's got a problem."
  • A source familiar with Trump's thinking said the president wants nothing to do with the brothers.
  • "The Tates want to pretend they were responsible for the president's victory [in 2024], but they weren't part of our strategy and the president doesn't know them," a former Trump campaign adviser said.

Flashback: After Andrew Tate first faced rape allegations in the U.K. in 2015 the brothers moved to Romania, where they began running their online porn business, according to a damning long-form investigation by the New Yorker called "Andrew Tate's Empire of Abuse."

  • When Trump won his first election in 2016, Andrew Tate posted supportive MAGA tweets and began messaging the president's oldest son, Donald Trump Jr.
  • Tate's online profile grew amid a masculine backlash to the 2018 #MeToo movement. His online courses sought to teach young men how to profit from turning women into "sex slaves," and awarded "PhD's" that stood for "Pimpin' Hos Degree."

As criminal investigations into the Tates grew, the brothers drew a parallel with the "lawfare" that Trump said he faced while running for reelection in 2023. During that time, Andrew Tate sat for softball interviews with podcasters Tucker Carlson and Candace Owens. Trump gave a Truth Social shoutout to Tristan Tate.

  • After an assassination attempt on Trump in 2024, Andrew Tate told reporters, "I'm very close with the Trump family. I know them well." He said he spoke with Trump's youngest son, Barron, and called the president "a bulletproof badass."

The intrigue: A month after Trump returned to office last year, Romanian authorities reinstated the Tate brothers' right to travel outside of the country as prosecutors reexamined procedural issues with their case.

  • Romania's foreign minister denied that the decision was linked to pressure from a Trump adviser, Ric Grenell, who had spoken favorably of the Tates. Grenell told Axios the minister broached the topic of the Tates with him and he made no demands.
  • Shortly afterward, the Tates flew from Romania on a private plane to Fort Lauderdale, Fla., where Customs and Border Patrol officers seized their phones.
  • The Tates got their phones back, however, thanks to the intervention of their former lawyer, Paul Ingrassia, who then was a White House liaison to the Department of Homeland Security, according to Pro Publica. Ingrassia told Axios the report was inaccurate.

Inside the room: Last week the Tates were in D.C., where they met with some members of Congress and rubbed elbows with insiders at the exclusive club, The Ned. There, they ran into Trump confidant and special envoy Paulo Zampolli, the Daily Mail first reported.

  • Zampolli invited the Tates to join 150 guests at his July 15 "summer soiree" at Zampolli's Dupont Circle home.
  • Zampolli told Axios he'd met the Tates three times before, starting at the Milken Institute Global Conference this year in Los Angeles, where he sat for a friendly interview on Andrew Tate's podcast.
  • "I did not know these allegations about them," Zampolli said. "That is on me."

What they're saying: One attendee at Zampolli's party said it was attended by people from the Justice, State and Treasury departments, as well as D.C. insiders and even some World Cup soccer players.

  • "The Tate brothers were like celebrities. People wanted to take pictures with them," the source said. "You never would've known they were about to get arrested."

item.title: U.S. measles cases surpass last year's total: Tracker
item.description:
The U.S. measles case count for this year has surged past last year's total and now stands at 2,295 — a level that hasn't been seen in 35 years, according to a Johns Hopkins University tracker that compiles state and local health data.

Why it matters: It's the latest sign that the virus is rebounding in areas with low vaccine coverage, threatening the United States' measles elimination status, which is due to be reviewed in November.

The big picture: The majority of cases are in unvaccinated people. While overall measles vaccination rates are still relatively high, public health officials say they must remain above 95% to maintain herd immunity.

By the numbers: As of Tuesday, there were nine more cases than in all of 2025, per the Johns Hopkins U.S. measles tracker.

  • Jurisdictions including South Carolina, Utah, Texas, Florida and Arizona have the most reported cases.
  • The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 2,260 confirmed cases in its last update on July 16. The agency said there were 34 new outbreaks reported this year.
  • The last time measles cases were higher was in 1991, when the U.S. had 9,643 cases, according to CDC data.

Threat level: Measles symptoms include a cough, high fever and conjunctivitis as well as a telltale rash, but can escalate into complications such as severe ear infections, pneumonia and encephalitis or inflammation of the brain that can lead to permanent brain damage and even death, per Johns Hopkins Medicine.

  • On average, measles kills between 1 and 3 of every 1,000 infected children.

The rebound comes at a time when a number of key top government health positions — including CDC director and surgeon general — remain vacant, and after Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. initially downplayed the virus' threat.

  • He's since said the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles spread while noting vaccination is a personal choice.

item.title: Senate rabble-rousers are gaining power
item.description:
Hardline conservatives are gaining power in the Senate atop key committees.

Why it matters: The senators known for rankling GOP leadership now have gavels that let them hold hearings, advance legislation and even issue subpoenas.

Driving the news: Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) will be the new chair of the Budget Committee, Senate Republicans agreed in their closed-door lunch Tuesday.

  • The committee, which has a key role in reconciliation, had been chaired by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.)
  • Johnson also chairs the Homeland Security subcommittee on investigations, allowing him to launch probes into everything from former President Biden's health to Meta's alleged cooperation with China.

What to watch: Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) is next in line to take the gavel on the powerful Judiciary Committee next Congress, following Graham's death and Sen. John Cornyn's (R-Texas) primary loss.

  • Lee would have to forfeit his current Energy Committee chair post.
  • He indicated to the Washington Examiner he would be willing to do so.

Zoom out: Fiscal hawk Rand Paul (R-Ky.) chairs the Homeland Security Committee, where he has been skeptical of massive agency budgets.

  • He recently voted "no" on Markwayne Mullin's nomination to be DHS secretary.
  • Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) chairs the Aging Committee, and he also leads the GOP steering committee, an unofficial, conservative group.
  • Scott has leveraged the group's weekly lunch to bring in top government officials, including President Trump, to discuss current issues.

The bottom line: The Senate runs on seniority. That means even senators willing to buck their party or criticize leadership can climb committee ranks.

item.title: Scoop: Progressives scorch Gillibrand over crypto
item.description:
Progressive groups are opening a vicious new front in the fight over crypto legislation, targeting Sen Kirsten Gillibrand as she tries to broker a compromise on the CLARITY Act, which has unresolved issues on its ethics provisions.

Why it matters: The blistering — and deeply personal — attack from Indivisible, Demand Progress and the Revolving Door Project complicates already delicate negotiations.

  • It's also a warning shot to Democrats: Progressive groups are prepared to make support for the bill politically painful, even if it means another bruising intraparty fight over one of the crypto industry's top legislative priorities.
  • "Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), is a prime example of a Democratic leader whose conduct undermines efforts to hold the Trump administration accountable for their rampant corruption," the groups wrote in a letter sent to every Democratic Senate office Tuesday evening.
  • "Fair or not, criticisms of the Trump administration's overwhelming corruption fall flat when voters perceive the critics to be engaged in substantively similar behavior."

The groups argue that Gillibrand's son's involvement in an equity trading platform leaves Democrats vulnerable to the very charge they are trying to level against President Trump.

  • Trump's crypto ventures have generated an estimated $600 million windfall, testing long-standing norms around presidents profiting from businesses affected by government decisions.

The other side: Gillibrand has called for Congress to prevent all elected officials, and their spouses, from issuing or sponsoring their own digital assets.

  • "This is a commonsense requirement that should get broad bipartisan support — public officials and their spouses should not be issuing memecoins," she said in a June statement.

State of play: Finding 60 votes for the CLARITY Act this summer is a high-wire act, but passing the bill remains a top priority for Senate Republicans, the White House and the crypto industry.

  • Sens. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) are working with the White House on compromise language for the ethics provisions. They appear to be making progress, though the details of the compromise haven't been released.
  • In addition to the talks with the White House, bipartisan talks are underway, with Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) leading Republicans in negotiating the ethics language.

The intrigue: Looming over the negotiations is the crypto industry's political war chest. Fairshake, its flagship super PAC, has some $125 million on hand.

  • The industry's political muscle gives both parties another incentive to reach a deal — and another reason for progressives to dig in.
  • Republicans are eager to put that money to work to help defend their Senate majority, but — as with the legislative negotiations — the clock is ticking for those dollars to have maximum impact in the midterm elections.

What we're hearing: Both parties view the ethics language as the biggest remaining obstacle to securing the 60 votes needed to pass the CLARITY Act.

  • The bill cleared the Senate Banking Committee in May with support from two Democrats, Sens. Ruben Gallego (Ariz.) and Angela Alsobrooks (Md.), underscoring the bill's bipartisan potential and the difficult coalition it will take to reach the Senate floor.

Zoom out: Crypto regulation continues to divide Democrats on both policy and politics.

  • Last year's passage of the GENIUS Act — which established the first federal regulatory framework for dollar-backed stablecoins — sparked tense internal Democratic debates over both the merits of the legislation and Trump's financial ties to the crypto industry.
  • In the end, 18 Senate Democrats voted for the bill.

Editor's note: This story has been updated to clarify that Gillibrand's son is involved with an equity trading platform (and not directly with the crypto industry).

item.title: World Cup final draws record 62.8M U.S. viewers
item.description:
Sunday's FIFA World Cup final drew more than 62.8 million viewers in the U.S., making it the most-watched World Cup final and soccer telecast in American history.

Why it matters: The record audience underscores soccer's growing popularity in the U.S. and is likely to boost the value of future media rights.

By the numbers: The game, which saw Spain beat defending champion Argentina 1–0 in extra time, also was the most-watched soccer match in Spanish-language media history, Telemundo said.

  • Nearly 39 million U.S. viewers watched the game on Fox, which had exclusive English-language broadcast rights in the U.S. Those figures are up 132% from the 2022 final on Fox, the company said.
  • Another nearly 24 million U.S. viewers tuned into the broadcast on Telemundo, which had exclusive Spanish-language broadcast rights in the U.S. Those figures are up 166% from the 2022 final on Telemundo.
Data: Nielsen; Note: Includes English and Spanish broadcasts. Nielsen began including out-of-home and streaming viewing in its official national TV ratings in 2020; Chart: Kerry Flynn/Axios

Streaming played a big role in the tournament's reach. June was the biggest subscriber acquisition month for Fox's streaming service, Fox One, according to Antenna.

  • Fox One added an estimated 2.8 million new subscribers in June, more than 2.5 times its previous monthly record in January during the NFL playoffs, per Antenna.
  • Nearly all of Fox's new June subscribers — 93% — were first-time customers rather than returning users.

The intrigue: Peacock, which streams Telemundo, also saw strong subscriber growth, recording an estimated 3.75 million U.S. sign-ups in June, per Antenna.

  • Streaming accounted for nearly half of Telemundo's World Cup audience, up from 30% in 2022, per Telemundo.
  • Telemundo's coverage resonated beyond Spanish speakers, as some preferred the energetic commentary, lack of commercials during the hydration breaks and cheaper cost of Peacock compared to Fox One.

Between the lines: America hosting the tournament, a competitive U.S. men's national team and broader streaming distribution helped push viewership to new heights in the U.S.

  • The U.S. team's matches set audience records. Fox said the U.S. opening match against Paraguay on June 12 became the most-watched FIFA Men's World Cup telecast in English-language U.S. history, averaging 18 million viewers.
  • The U.S. men's victory over Bosnia and Herzegovina on July 1 set the record as the biggest English-language TV audience for any soccer match in America with 26.4 million viewers on Fox.
  • The U.S. team's loss to Belgium on July 6 later bested the record with 37.2 million viewers on Fox, per Nielsen, along with 12.9 million viewers on Telemundo, for more than 50 million combined.
  • The July 5 match between Mexico and England came close to that record with 46.7 million viewers on Fox and Telemundo.

The big picture: The FIFA World Cup has historically attracted the largest global audience of any recurring television event worldwide.

  • FIFA has not yet released worldwide figures. The 2022 World Cup final between Argentina and France held the previous final game viewership record at 1.42 billion worldwide, per FIFA.
  • Live sports remain one of the few programming categories capable of attracting massive live audiences, driving both advertising revenue and streaming subscriptions.
  • FIFA also experimented with bringing more American-style entertainment to the event, including its first halftime show for a World Cup final, to help the tournament appeal beyond traditional soccer fans.

What to watch: FIFA is expected to cash in on the tournament's success by opening up the media rights bidding process for the 2030 World Cup.

  • Fox and Telemundo's current agreements ran through the 2026 tournament, after FIFA extended the deals without a competitive bidding process for the 2022 tournament.
  • FIFA has reportedly alerted media companies that English- and Spanish-language U.S. rights are likely to be sold together as a package for 2030, per CNBC, with Netflix, Disney and YouTube all interested in bidding.

item.title: Scoop: Trump's top MAGA advisers gather to plot midterms
item.description:
President Trump's top political advisers inside and outside of the White House are meeting Tuesday afternoon to review polling, their messaging and strategy ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.

Why it matters: Trump's super PAC and the Republican National Committee are sitting on about $530 million, and now his team is figuring out how, when and where to deploy it.

  • That doesn't include what insiders say is hundreds of millions of dollars more in Trump's dark-money political nonprofit, Securing American Greatness.

Zoom in: The meeting at the Four Seasons hotel in D.C. is the second of what are becoming regular Trump team conclaves to coordinate the GOP, its candidates and his political operation. Trump won't be there, but these top MAGA shot-callers will be:

  • Tony Fabrizio, Trump's longtime top pollster, who will give a presentation about the midterm picture.
  • James Blair, Trump's hands-on political operations chief in charge of executing a midterm plan.
  • Susie Wiles, White House chief of staff and Trump's longest-serving political adviser.
  • Chris LaCivita, Trump's former campaign co-manager with Wiles.
  • Joe Gruters, RNC chair under Trump and a longtime ally of Wiles.
  • Cabinet officials (except Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who's in Manila on official business).

Zoom out: Republicans acknowledge it will be tough to maintain control of the U.S. House with Trump's poll numbers bottoming out amid rising gas prices and the war in Iran.

  • But Trump's political operatives say voters are wary of Democrats' progressive overreach, and they think this election will be about who Americans hate more, not who they love.
  • Republicans also sparked an unprecedented round of mid-decade redistricting that could net the GOP 10 additional House seats, making that chamber easier to defend.

Yes, but: Trump is fighting political gravity. With few exceptions, a president whose party controls both chambers of Congress usually loses control of at least one in a midterm election.

  • Polls show voters don't believe the economy is in good shape and are blaming Trump.
  • "Voters feel that Trump's economic policies have made things worse — because they have," John Anzalone, a top Democratic pollster who also surveys for the Wall Street Journal, wrote last week on X.

What they're saying: "The Trump tax cuts have saved people real money and the president is keeping Americans safe," said one Trump operative involved in Tuesday's meeting.

  • "We have the manpower, the message and the money to make that clear."

item.title: Scoop: Trump's Cabinet members are joining TikTok after DOJ shift
item.description:
Most of President Trump's Cabinet will launch TikTok accounts Tuesday, a move that comes days after the Justice Department told federal employees it was safe to use the app because of its sale to a U.S.-approved owner.

Why it matters: The move is a striking shift from Trump's first term, when his administration argued that TikTok posed a national security threat because of its ownership by China's ByteDance.

  • By joining the app themselves, Cabinet officials are effectively signaling that TikTok is now an acceptable venue for government messaging.

The background: The 2022 No TikTok on Government Devices Act said TikTok couldn't be used on government-issued phones.

  • But Trump's DOJ now says that law is no longer applicable, given the change in the company's ownership to a U.S.-controlled venture earlier year.

Zoom in: Trump's administration now views TikTok as a powerful tool for reaching young voters.

  • Trump himself has been on the app since 2024, and some of his posts — including one documenting his appearance at a UFC event — have gotten hundreds of millions of views.
